summary: A definition of the Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol from the Network Graphics Working Group, written by Ira Cotton of MITRE. All input is described by type, origin and length followed by the data. Level 0 defines two input types, text and simple position, and lists device codes such as keyboard, tablet, mouse and lightpen.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 336 defines a basic format for graphics input sent over the network. Each message says what kind of input it carries, which device produced it and how much data follows.

subtitle: A simple message format for graphics input

tldr.problem: Graphics systems need a consistent way to describe input from devices such as keyboards and pointing devices.
tldr.mechanism: Level 0 messages identify the input type, the originating device and the amount of following data before carrying the data.
tldr.outcome: The document defines formats for text and simple position input and directs other input to a different link.

today: RFC 336 defines a Level 0 graphics input format with two input types. The document does not describe later levels or a broader graphics protocol.

sections.title: A Common Structure for Input
sections.content:
The Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol describes each input by its type, its origin and its length, followed by the data itself. It defines only two kinds of input: text and simple position information.

Device codes identify sources such as a primary keyboard, tablet, mouse, joystick, lightpen, cursor or keyset. Code 0 means that the device is unspecified.
sections.plainLanguage: Every input message identifies what it contains, which device sent it and how much data follows. Level 0 covers text and position information.

sections.title: Text and Position Messages
sections.content:
A text message uses the TEXTIN code, a device code, a character count and then a string of network ASCII characters. A position message uses POSIT, a device code, a byte count and then x and y coordinates.

At Level 0, the position count is always four bytes: two bytes for each coordinate. The coordinates are signed fractions, following the representation used by the Level 0 graphic output protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A text message gives the length of its text. A position message gives the size of its two coordinates, with two bytes for each coordinate.

sections.title: Input Outside the Level 0 Format
sections.content: The protocol covers only the two defined Level 0 formats. The RFC says input that does not fit these formats should travel on a different link from the graphics input link. It notes that this separation may be useful when the extra protocol overhead is not wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: If an input does not match the text or position format, send it on another link. This avoids using the Level 0 format for data it does not describe.
